title: Antonelli wins in US but has to wait to secure title
text:
Kimi Antonelli just missed out on clinching his first world title in a dominant victory in the United States Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old Italian leads Mercedes team-mate George Russell by 123 points after coming home ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Antonelli will be crowned champion in Mexico City next weekend as long he does not lose more than 23 points to Russell or more than 24 to Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

That means a ninth place would be enough to become champion even if Russell wins the race, and a 10th would be enough if Hamilton is victorious.

If Russell or Hamilton do not win, Antonelli will be champion next Sunday no matter where he finishes.

Antonelli stamped his authority on this race in the same way as he has on the season, and was out of touch even by the first corner as his rivals all battled behind him at the Circuit of the Americas.

Antonelli's sublime victory, his first since the Spanish Grand Prix last month

A race-long squabble between Leclerc and Verstappen for second place

Antonelli took control of the race from the very beginning, an excellent start combined with a gripping scrap through the first lap between Verstappen and Leclerc leaving him more than two seconds clear by the end of the first lap.

Mercedes had chosen the medium tyres for the start, while Leclerc and the Red Bulls of Verstappen and Isack Hadjar started on new softs.

And Antonelli was able to convert that choice into a one-stop race while almost everyone else did two, emphasising his superiority as he finished 16 seconds clear of Leclerc.

The race was also a stamp of approval for the Mercedes upgrade package that was introduced two races ago in Malaysia but initially took them backwards.

Assiduous work ever since has moved it to the point where, while it remains tricky to optimise, it is definitively quicker than the older specification.

"It was the result we needed," Antonelli said. "All this time putting work on the new package and finally seeing the result was very pleasant, perfect strategy to call the one-stop."

As for the title, he said: "I know we are very close. We try to finish on a high and hopefully we can clinch it very soon."

Russell, who started sixth, had a frustrating race. He was given a five-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage, which dropped him to 10th after his pit stop. He could only make up two places and finished eighth.

Hamilton's fourth place means both he and fellow Briton Russell just about retain a mathematical chance of winning the championship.

The entertainment was provided by Leclerc and Verstappen, initially wheel to wheel and then at a distance as divergent strategies played out.

Leclerc, who started fourth, jumped up to third place behind Verstappen on the exit of the first corner, and then bravely sat it out around the outside of the Red Bull through the high speed Turn Three at the start of the Esses and then dived down the inside into Turn Four.

Verstappen, though, was not finished, and he closed in on Leclerc down the back straight and they fought hard through the switchback series of corners through the stadium section before the Dutchman claimed second place with a dive down the inside of Turn 15.

Verstappen led Leclerc to his first stop on lap 13, Ferrari waiting two laps longer before the Monegasque made his own first stop.

Verstappen went on to the soft tyres and Leclerc the mediums, the Dutchman then switching to mediums when he stopped on lap 31.

But Leclerc's mediums in the second stint allowed him to run eight laps longer than the Red Bull driver.

Leclerc came out 8.5 seconds behind the Dutchman and closed the gap to be on his tail within five laps as Verstappen himself came up behind Lando Norris' McLaren.

They ran nose to tail for two laps before Verstappen passed Norris into Turn One on lap 47, Leclerc following him past later in the lap.

Two laps later, Leclerc picked off Verstappen down the inside of Turn One to secure the second podium position.

Verstappen was grumbling about his car over the radio for much of the race but he had enough to hold off a late charge from Hamilton - on a similar strategy to Leclerc - by one second at the flag.

Norris managed to nurse his tyres to the end with just one stop to beat Hadjar, while the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri fended off Russell for half the race to take seventh.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alpine's Pierre Gasly claimed the final points positions in ninth and 10th.

1996 world champion Damon Hill on BBC Radio 5 Live

Kimi Antonelli has an infectious personality. The team love him, he's enjoying everything he's got in F1 and he's very grateful for all the breaks they've given him at Mercedes. But he delivers. He's such a nice kid. It's incredible - 20 years old and he's on the verge of winning his first championship, which I'm sure will be the first of many.

F1 moves south from Texas for the Mexico City Grand Prix next weekend, from 30 October-1 November. It is likely to be the scene of Antonelli's crowning as the sport's youngest world champion.

title: End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd fans make clear who they blame
text:
There was an air of inevitability about Michael Carrick's walk around Old Trafford after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth .

It is not unusual for Carrick to applaud the Manchester United fans. If anything, his acknowledgements were not as pronounced as they were in Como after the equally devastating loss.

But after eight games without a win, the worst run since 2015-16 and two horrific defeats in a week, the end is approaching for Carrick, with his bosses in serious talks about his future.

However, if anyone in a senior position at the club thinks the issues at Old Trafford will be solved simply by changing the head coach and, more importantly, the fans will be appeased by a new face in the dugout, the reaction from the stands on an awful day on and off the pitch would have very clearly told them otherwise.

On Friday, as he looked back on that 4-1 loss to Como and ahead to Bournemouth , Carrick said: "We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."

Carrick could not answer if he will still be in charge for next Saturday's trip to Chelsea . He does not know.

"The responsibility is mine," he said. "What else can I say really right now? I totally understand the situation. I'm not expecting anything either way. I love this place and I'll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club."

Fernandes left on bench for Man Utd defeat - a failed gamble?

Carrick future under major threat - can he survive?

United's fans delivered their own verdict on the performance as Carrick disappeared down the tunnel to the dressing room.

After repeatedly singing the former midfielder's name, as soon as he was out of view they turned on the players. The booing lasted until the last of them, Diogo Dalot, left the pitch. They simply feel they are either not good enough or don't care enough, or both.

The game was less than a minute old when the first anti-Glazer and anti-Sir Jim Ratcliffe songs were heard.

The Glazer family have been public enemy number one among the United faithful ever since their leveraged takeover in 2005.

The debt they initially landed on the club has now grown to over £1.15bn, according to their latest accounts. The amount it has cost in interest is £852m, according to respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble. In the last financial year, the interest payment was £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.

The argument is, that money could have been used far more productively to sign better players.

There had been hope Ratcliffe, a boyhood United fan, would change that when he struck a deal with the Glazers to become a minority shareholder on Christmas Eve 2023.

Instead, a succession of decisions have led to major questions over his handling of the club.

On the management side, United's hierarchy eventually backed Erik ten Hag after talking with alternatives in the wake of the shock 2024 FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City , spending over £200m on the likes of Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt and Manuel Ugarte.

Last week, Ten Hag told the Athletic , external the club went back on a promise not to sell homegrown Scotland international Scott McTominay to fund Ugarte's £50m move from Paris St-Germain. They sacked the Dutchman in October 2024.

After that they persuaded Ruben Amorim to leave Sporting mid-season, when he wanted to wait until the summer.

They stuck with him after an unprecedented 15th-place finish, and again after United lost to League Two Grimsby in the EFL Cup, then sacked him in January when he clashed with director of football Jason Wilcox over playing style.

That led to Carrick's arrival to the end of the season, which turned into a permanent appointment after he guided the club back into the Champions League after a two-year absence.

A third dismissal in three seasons would not reflect well on anyone.

The 'Standards' banner that was held up on the Stretford End showing the images of legendary skippers Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and Roy Keane was there to remind the executives running the club of the history they should be aspiring to.

Wilcox has largely operated behind the scenes but he could not fail to hear the obscenities being sung against him during today's game, nor the boos as he climbed into the vehicle taking him away from the stadium nearly two hours after the final whistle.

Recruited from a similar role at Southampton following the Ratcliffe takeover and elevated in status following the dismissal of Dan Ashworth, amid the decision to recruit Amorim, the 55-year-old is blamed by many fans for the club's recent recruitment, even though the budget was set at a much higher level.

Sat next to him at Old Trafford to watch the Bournemouth debacle unfold was chief executive Omar Berrada, who worked with Wilcox at Manchester City .

Having senior figures steeped in City's recent history was always a potential problem if results didn't go well. Berrada played no part in the recent Premier League proceedings that found City guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, but the link is clear, and United's fans sang about that at Old Trafford as well.

If that wasn't enough, a ticket touting investigation launched in the summer led to condemnation from all United's major fan groups. The club argued they were trying to catch touts, while fans felt it was an attempt to drive regular match-goers out in favour of more corporate sales. The club are adamant that is not the case, but the argument is falling on deaf ears.

The same is also true of plans for a new 100,000-capacity stadium. The club conducted a survey which they said showed the majority of respondents were in favour of a new ground. The stadium is likely to cost in excess of £2bn and United spent £63.5m on land for it earlier this year.

Some supporters simply don't believe those figures. The Stretford End impolitely told Ratcliffe they had no interest in a new stadium as well today.…

title: Remco in the USA: Hanging Out with Fans, Scoping LA Olympics Course
author: sstokes
text:
Remco Evenepoel has had a interesting off season, visiting the US and also attending the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma in October 11, 2026. (Photo: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (Photo: NurPhoto)

It’s the off season, a time to recharge, but that hasn’t stopped Olympic and world TT champion Remco Evenepoel from logging more training kilometers and scoping out the route of a major objective.

The Belgian is currently in California visiting the headquarters of bike sponsor Specialized and has used that time to build relationships and to work on some things which could pay off well in 2027 and beyond.

On Sunday he put in a 65.34km ride, starting near Griffith Park and the LA Zoo, and taking in parts of the TT course for the 2028 LA Olympic Games.

The full route has not yet been released but he still used the time to familiarize himself with the area and with whatever course details he has been able to ascertain.

The ride then concluded close to the beach at Santa Monica.

Evenepoel has been busy since arriving in LA, doing what he described as a LA Jetlag and Sunrise Run on Saturday and then taking in a 48.08km social ride with Specialized.

Photos from the latter were posted by @Shreddypendergrass, and showed Evenepoel doing a group ride in his European road champion’s jersey.

Also present were FDJ Suez riders Demi Vollering and Kate Courtney . The world champ and US national champion are also Specialized-sponsored athletes.

According to Sporza, the trip will see Evenepoel—and presumably the other pros—do additional wind tunnel testing at the Specialized HQ in Morgan Hill.

The Belgian recently spent some days at a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe training camp, working on plans for next season.

He had his best season to date in 2026, notching up 15 victories including the worlds TT and European championships road race, and taking the runner-up slot in the Tour de France.

Vollering had an even more impressive year, taking 16 wins in 33 days of competition. Her triumphs included the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, the Giro d’Italia Women, the world road championships, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Tour of Flanders and more.

Both are highly ambitious and, like Courtney, are using this time to work towards even bigger results next year.

title: The 2027 Tour de France Femmes Route Design Beats the Men’s Race, and It’s Not Even Close
author: sstokes
text:
Demi Vollering won the Tour de France Femmes for the second time this year (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

It lacks high altitude climbs but the route of next year’s Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift does something the men’s event doesn’t do.

The profiles of both races were unveiled Thursday in Paris by organizer ASO. Something that was immediately apparent was that the expected contest between Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas and others runs the risk of fizzling out days before the conclusion in Paris.

This year stage 20 saw the riders duke it out to the summit of Alpe d’Huez, facing one of the Tour’s most notorious climbs on two successive days.

Pogačar was sufficiently far ahead by then to have the yellow jersey sewn up, but the battle for the podium still raged. Isaac del Toro ultimately distanced Seixas close to the finish and seal third overall.

Next summer? There is a danger of an anti-climax, with the last big mountain battle coming on stage 18’s summit finish at Saint Larry Soulan. The following stage does offer three climbs yet the highest of those, the Col de Soudet, is just 1540 meters above sea level and tops out 65km from the finish.

It is followed by the final categorized climb of the race, the Col de Marie Blanque. It’s a well-known peak, but while it is steep it is just 7.7km in duration and summits a full 18.5km from the finish line.

That’s not exactly a showdown, and the issue is compounded with a sprinters’ day out on stage 20 and a Montmartre-enhanced concluder in Paris which will offer good racing, but may well see the GC neutralized again.

All together, there is a danger the men’s Tour de France could end with a whimper, not a bang.

Fortunately, the same can’t be said of the Tour de France Femmes.

The Femmes race debuted in 2022 and has offered some of the best competition in pro cycling. Just consider the 2024 edition, which was every bit as much a cliffhanger as the conclusion of the men’s 1989 Tour.

Kasia Niewiadoma started the day in yellow, was dropped on the Col du Glandon, but fought all the way to the summit of Alpe d’Huez to win by just five seconds overall.

That was even closer than the classic 1989 showdown where Greg LeMond overhauled Laurent Fignon by eight seconds.

Last year’s race saw Pauline Ferrand Prétot stamp her authority all over the event, easily dropping her rivals in the mountains on the final two days. And while the Frenchwoman did have a 2:37 minute lead going into the final stage, the fact that it was a summit finish meant that there was—theoretically at least—the possibility that Vollering and others could turn things around.

The drama continued this summer when Vollering and Niewiadoma went into the hilly concluder in Nice a mere eight seconds apart.

It was, once again, a nailbiter, and left the outcome undecided right until the finale.

That kind of suspense will continue next summer, thanks to another well thought out route design. The race will again build steadily towards a crescendo, maintaining suspense in a way that the men’s Tour likely won’t.

In trying to avoid another Tadej Pogačar domination, the organizers have neutered things in a way that could backfire.

The Femmes course design avoids that problem. It’s not quite perfect, but it should be very entertaining.

As detailed by Velo’s Andy Hood this week, the Femmes route will begin in Leeds and offers three days of high-stakes racing on British soil. Day one heads to Manchester and takes in 85.7km of rolling terrain. Stage two crams nearly 3000 altitude meters of punchy racing into a 154.4km route to Sheffield, while stage three will be a tricky 18km team time trial in London.

That nervous start will be followed by three complicated transition stages on French soil, to Calais, Magnanville and Bourges respectively. Those offer something for the sprinters, but also for the attackers. Stage 5 in particular could be a puncheurs’ delight, with series of short, steep climbs in the final hour and a half of racing.

The GC battle really comes into focus on the final three stages. Stage 7 is almost completely flat for the first 100km but then concludes with a summit finish to the top of La Loge des Gardes. Sure, the final climb is just 6.7km but it is preceded by a tricky uphill approach which should see some very nervous racing.

Stage 8 is continuously up and down. It does lack a summit finish but 3000 meters of altitude gain en route to Clermont-Ferrand will lead to a lot of tension, particularly if time gaps are tight.

The big decider is stage nine’s summit finish to the top of the Puy de Dôme. The climb is an iconic one, most famous for a literal shoulder to shoulder battle between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor in 1964.

Those slopes were closed to the Tour for many years but made a return to the men’s race in 2023, when Michael Woods won and Tadej Pogačar dropped Jonas Vingegaard, only to lose out overall.

It’s not as long or as tough as other iconic mountains in cycling but everything in the race builds towards this big showdown. And while fans were not allowed on the climb three years ago for the men’s Tour, there are suggestions this could change next summer.

It should be another gripping finale to the Tour de France Femmes, guaranteeing GC suspense right to the closing minutes. It’s something the men’s race should aspire to too yet, next year at least, almost certainly won’t.

That’s a shame for the men’s Tour. At least the Femmes will keep everyone guessing right until the end.

VIDEO: Tadej Pogačar Slammed for ‘Reckless Riding’ in Monaco
author: Jim Cotton
text:
(Photo: Getty Images / Noah Alfrink Instagram)

Tadej Pogačar heard the Tour de France director questioning his appetite for risk after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España and said, “Hold my beer.”

Fan footage shot last week showing the 28-year-old slalom through traffic in busy Monaco suggests Pogi has bounced back confident as ever.

The videos, filmed Thursday and shared on Instagram by French amateur Noah Alfrink, are a white-knuckle watch.

The grabs show Pogačar resplendent in his UAE Emirates-XRG jersey cutting lanes, squeezing alongside buses, and flirting with the bumpers of moving cars in the hectic roads of his adopted home.

The videos went viral this weekend and have drawn a very mixed response.

Not even the GOATed fan favorite is spared from criticism of “reckless riding,” a “lack of respect for safety,” and a whole lot more. The 19-year-old Alfrink isn’t shown mercy either, as commentators hit out at the latest example of fans “ cyclo-stalking ” superstar riders.

“I don’t know which is dumber, Pogačar, or the one following him,” reads one comment.

Imágenes de un aficionado siguiendo a Tadej Pogačar durante su entrenamiento de ayer por Mónaco ➡️ El esloveno iba vestido con el maillot del UAE 📹 @noah_alfr pic.twitter.com/fs0nr6sbxI

Only one day earlier, Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme pondered whether Pogačar would be the same after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España.

The 28-year-old broke his collarbone, a vertebra, and suffered a concussion when he hit the tarmac hard in late August.

It cost the Tour de France dominator the chance to win the Vuelta’s red jersey, defend his titles at the world and European championships, and win a sixth Il Lombardia.

Speaking to L’Equipe on Thursday, Prudhomme questioned whether the crash pierced Pogačar’s sense of invincibility, too.

“The real question for me – and I obviously wish him well – is how well he’ll have recovered from his very, very, very serious crash in the Vuelta a España,” Prudhomme said. “His talent lies not only in his physical superiority, but also in his riding skills.

“His descent of the Tourmalet last summer was mind-blowing and jaw-dropping,” Prudhomme told L’Equipe . “As you get older, after such a massive crash, are you still the same person? Do you take as many risks?”

Prudhomme spoke the day he and ASO unleashed a route for the 2027 Tour de France that’s been labeled “anti-Pogačar.”

The race director suggested 71km of time trialing might not be Pogačar’s only problem when he defends his yellow jersey next July.

“There are certainly questions lingering after his crash,” Prudhomme said. “Whether it has left its mark on him and what the consequences will be.

Pogačar seems to have brushed off any mental hangover of his 60kph crash just fine.

Some may say his comfort on the bike might be a little too good.

Pogačar, his teammates, and the staff at UAE Emirates-XRG meet next for a 2027 planning and admin camp. It doesn’t look like Pogačar will be nervous in the wheels of any group rides.

title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says
author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
text:
Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup , the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London . While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham .

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit . Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won . She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims . Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

title: Briton Palmowski wins F1 Academy title
text:
Britain's Alisha Palmowski says that winning the F1 Academy title is "a dream come true".

The 20-year-old finished second in Saturday's reverse grid race at the Circuit of the Americas, which was enough to be crowned champion before Sunday's feature race and the season finale in Las Vegas in November.

Palmowski becomes the youngest champion of the all-female development series, and is the second British driver to win the title after Abbi Pulling in 2024.

She drives for Campos Racing and is part of the Red Bull driver academy.

Glossop-born Palmowski has won five out of the 11 races held so far this season, only finishing outside of the points once during the reverse grid race at Zandvoort.

In an emotional post-race interview, she dedicated her championship win to her ill grandmother and thanked her family.

"It's been a really special journey. I started racing when I was eight or nine years old, it was just me and my parents," she said.

"The sacrifices that they've made behind the scenes, they've really put their lives on pause to allow me to live my dream."

Before Saturday's race, Austrian Emma Felbermayr was the only driver with a mathematical chance of overhauling Palmowski but fourth place was not enough to keep her hopes alive.

Denmark's Alba Larsen took the chequered flag to secure her first F1 Academy victory, with 17-year-old Lisa Billard of France completing the podium in third.

title: Antonelli stands on brink of history in Austin
text:
Kimi Antonelli stands on the brink of history at the United States Grand Prix, where he can become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history on Sunday, but far from feeling the pressure he says he is enjoying himself more than usual.

It certainly looked like it on Saturday at the Circuit of the Americas as he took a surprise pole position by 0.179 seconds from Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli will become world champion on Sunday if he wins the race while his Mercedes team-mate George Russell is lower than eighth and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton below fourth.

Hamilton and Russell start the race fifth and sixth.

Antonelli had not been on pole since the Belgian Grand Prix in July after Mercedes' early season dominance came under challenge from first McLaren and then Red Bull. And his delight was clear as he whooped over the team radio on his slowing down lap.

Antonelli takes US pole on weekend he can win title

He came into the weekend insisting he was going to try to apply the "same mindset as I had all year - one race at a time".

But on Saturday he acknowledged that this one was a new kind of weekend.

"It does feel a little bit different," he said. "But the goal stays the same. I just need to keep doing my job. And, actually, I feel like I can enjoy more driving, everything.

"But, of course, we're going to do the race tomorrow. We're going to try and win. And then we'll see what happens. Obviously, I'm in a very good position."

Antonelli is typically accompanied by his father, Marco, at grands prix, but he said this weekend he had brought other people with him as well to help keep him in the right frame of mind.

"I have a great group of people around me," he said. "I have a lot of friends here as well, so we enjoy the evenings together.

"We play cards in the evening, so we're just doing the fun stuff. And that's what helps, to just relax a little bit and just connect with the mind, and then once you go on track you are back full focus."

The maths suggest the most likely scenario is that Antonelli will not win the title on Sunday - it would, as he put it on Thursday, require "something catastrophic to happen to the others".

If this is a bit of an overstatement - Russell and Hamilton would need only to crash together on the first lap, for example - the fundamental truth is real.

He has such a huge advantage - he is 102 points clear of Russell and 111 ahead of Hamilton - that the championship is an inevitability at some point, as Verstappen pointed out when he was asked if he had any advice for his young friend before the race.

"He doesn't need that," the four-time world champion said. "He knows what he's doing. He just needs to try and win the race. If it doesn't happen here, it will happen next weekend (in Mexico City). If it doesn't happen next weekend, it will happen the weekend after (in Sao Paulo).

"It's just been an incredible season. So, you have to also just try and enjoy, of course, this kind of ride over the last months that you've been in. And at one point it's official, and then you can celebrate."

"Incredible" is an over-used word, but an entirely appropriate one in the circumstances.

When it happens, Antonelli will beat the record for youngest champion by more than three years - he will be 20 years and 61 days old on Sunday and Sebastian Vettel, the current record holder, was 23 years and 133 days old when he won his first title in 2010.

Antonelli has taken this season by storm, taking eight victories in the 17 races so far, including a run of five in a row after Russell won the first grand prix of the year in Australia.

In doing so, he has dramatically turned the tables after a shaky maiden season in 2025 in which flashes of promise interspersed a generally disappointing year in the context of him being hailed before his debut as a potential generational talent.

This year, he has looked every bit that, but that does not mean a victory on Sunday is a foregone conclusion.

His pole was a surprise because the people most likely to achieve it before qualifying had appeared to be one of the Ferrari drivers or Verstappen.

But Ferrari faded, as they so often do, Charles Leclerc complaining about his tyres losing grip as the sun and temperature dropped, Hamilton saying: "The car felt really good. The lap was solid, so they were just quicker."

Verstappen, meanwhile, went into the final session with "high hopes" after setting a competitive time on used tyres in the second session, only to find his grip had evaporated in the final session.

The race, though, is a different matter. Verstappen's race pace was strong on Friday and he said: "Yes, we have been happier in the long runs. And I hope that it will be the same tomorrow."

Leclerc said he believed he could battle for the win if he could make a good start but Hamilton was not so sure.

He said: "You have to be realistic. We're fourth and fifth. It's very hard to overtake here. Even if you're P2 on the grid, it's hard to beat someone (on pole) over a race distance. I raced here since 2012. It took a lot to get past Vettel back then. But maybe with strategy, we can progress."

There's really only one story on Sunday, though. Antonelli will be champion sooner or later. Which will it be?
